title: A Survey on Computer-Aided Diagnosis for Ocular Diseases

subsections.section_title: Ocular Imaging Modalities and Data Acquisition for Computer-Aided Diagnosis
subsections.subsection_title: Ocular Imaging Modalities and Data Acquisition for Computer-Aided Diagnosis - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Color fundus photography remains the most widely deployed imaging modality for computer-aided ophthalmic diagnosis because it provides a noninvasive, relatively low-cost two-dimensional record of the retina, optic disc, macula, and major vessels. Its digital acquisition pipeline has been extensively reviewed, including field-of-view, mydriatic versus non-mydriatic capture, illumination variability, and compression or resolution choices that directly affect lesion visibility and algorithm robustness ref [33]. In CAD systems, fundus images are particularly suited to detecting diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, vascular abnormalities, and glaucomatous optic disc changes through automated analysis of exudates, microaneurysms, hemorrhages, drusen, vessel caliber, and cup-to-disc morphology ref [3], ref [33].

From a data-acquisition perspective, fundus-based screening datasets are shaped by camera optics, operator expertise, motion blur, media opacity, and inter-device color inconsistency, all of which influence downstream segmentation and classification performance. Comparative screening studies have shown that digital imaging can provide clinically useful sensitivity for diabetic retinopathy detection and may outperform routine examination workflows in standardized settings, which helps explain its central role in teleophthalmology and large-scale CAD deployment ref [43]. Beyond conventional RGB imaging, modality extensions enrich the observable signal: fundus autofluorescence highlights lipofuscin-related metabolic alterations and has demonstrated characteristic spatial associations with drusen in age-related macular degeneration ref [35], while hyperspectral fundus imaging enables estimation of optic nerve head oxygen saturation and other spectrally derived biomarkers that may support functional disease assessment ref [47].

Although fundus photography is fundamentally projection-based and lacks intrinsic depth resolution, it serves as the entry point for multimodal CAD because it is easy to standardize and annotate at scale. Reviews of retinal image analysis emphasize that the modality has been foundational for automated vessel extraction, optic disc localization, lesion detection, and image quality assessment ref [3]. It is therefore best viewed as the baseline acquisition modality against which higher-dimensional techniques such as OCT and vascular imaging are integrated for more comprehensive computer-aided diagnosis ref [5], ref [10], ref [34].

subsections.section_title: Ocular Imaging Modalities and Data Acquisition for Computer-Aided Diagnosis
subsections.subsection_title: Ocular Imaging Modalities and Data Acquisition for Computer-Aided Diagnosis - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Color fundus photography remains a core acquisition modality for computer-aided diagnosis because it provides a two-dimensional view of the retina, optic disc, macula, and vascular tree at relatively low cost and high clinical accessibility. Its diagnostic utility is especially strong for diabetic retinopathy, hypertensive retinopathy, glaucoma screening, and vascular abnormality assessment, where lesion appearance and global retinal geometry can be inferred directly from image intensities and color contrasts. Recent hardware developments also broaden acquisition settings: portable and mobile-phone-based retinal cameras support wider field capture and community screening workflows, making fundus imaging increasingly relevant for scalable automated analysis in resource-limited environments ref [10].

From an algorithmic perspective, fundus images are particularly amenable to structural analysis of the optic nerve head and retinal vasculature. Classical optic disc localization methods frequently exploit the approximately circular bright appearance of the disc, for example through Hough-transform-based formulations for optic disk or optic nerve head detection ref [12], ref [52]. In parallel, vessel extraction and modeling have been extensively studied because the vascular network encodes biomarkers for both ocular and systemic disease. Representative approaches include multi-orientation vessel tracking, which is suited to elongated curvilinear structures across varying directions, and multiresolution Hermite modeling for capturing vessel profiles across scales ref [18], ref [41].

A further advantage of fundus photography for CAD is that it supports higher-level semantic analysis beyond simple lesion detection. Artery-vein classification from retinal images enables estimation of vessel caliber ratios, branching characteristics, and hemodynamic proxies relevant to diabetic retinopathy, hypertension, and cardiovascular risk stratification ref [14]. However, performance remains sensitive to acquisition quality, including uneven illumination, media opacity, narrow field of view, and variability across cameras. Consequently, data acquisition protocols, optic disc-centered versus macula-centered framing, and portable-device imaging characteristics must be considered jointly with algorithm design when developing robust fundus-based diagnostic systems ref [10], ref [12], ref [14], ref [18].

subsections.section_title: Ocular Imaging Modalities and Data Acquisition for Computer-Aided Diagnosis
subsections.subsection_title: Ocular Imaging Modalities and Data Acquisition for Computer-Aided Diagnosis - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) has become a central modality for computer-aided diagnosis because it provides cross-sectional, micrometer-scale visualization of retinal architecture in vivo. The transition from earlier OCT systems to broadband and three-dimensional acquisitions substantially improved axial resolution, volumetric coverage, and the ability to localize subtle pathology, making OCT especially suitable for automated assessment of macular, retinal nerve fiber layer, and vitreoretinal disorders ref [14], ref [35]. For CAD pipelines, these acquisition characteristics are important because they support both slice-wise analysis and full volumetric modeling of disease morphology.

A major data-acquisition consideration in OCT-based CAD is that the diagnostic signal is embedded in layered retinal anatomy. Consequently, segmentation of intraretinal boundaries and macular sublayers is a foundational step for quantitative analysis. Reviews of OCT retinal image segmentation highlight the diversity of algorithmic strategies developed for boundary detection, denoising, and layer delineation, while comparative studies of automated macular layer segmentation show how performance varies with image quality, pathology, and anatomical complexity ref [9], ref [30]. These observations directly affect dataset curation: reliable labels often require expert correction, and acquisition protocols must balance scan density, motion artifacts, and signal strength to preserve layer separability for downstream learning.

Beyond structural thickness estimation, OCT supports richer CAD targets through texture and microvascular analysis. Texture-based classification methods, including SVM-driven approaches, demonstrate that OCT reflectivity patterns can discriminate tissue states that are not fully captured by simple geometric measurements ref [32]. At the same time, ultrahigh-resolution OCT combined with adaptive optics enables imaging of retinal capillaries, extending OCT-derived data from structural profiling toward fine vascular phenotyping ref [34]. Together, these advances position OCT as a versatile modality for automated diagnosis, where acquisition settings, resolution, and volume design critically shape algorithm robustness and clinical applicability ref [14], ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Ocular Imaging Modalities and Data Acquisition for Computer-Aided Diagnosis
subsections.subsection_title: Ocular Imaging Modalities and Data Acquisition for Computer-Aided Diagnosis - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Fundus autofluorescence (FAF) provides a complementary imaging modality for computer-aided diagnosis by capturing the intrinsic emission of ocular fluorophores, primarily associated with retinal pigment epithelium metabolism. Compared with color fundus photography, FAF highlights functional and metabolic disturbance before overt structural change, making it valuable for automated detection, lesion delineation, and longitudinal monitoring in inherited, inflammatory, and degenerative retinal disorders. Near-infrared autofluorescence further extends this capability by probing signal sources with distinct spatial localization and biological significance, which is important when designing modality-specific preprocessing and feature extraction pipelines ref [25].

From a data-acquisition perspective, FAF supports quantitative analysis of lesion extent and progression. In Stargardt disease, autofluorescent imaging has been used to measure atrophic lesion growth, illustrating how standardized serial acquisition enables longitudinal computer-assisted tracking of disease burden ref [21]. Disease-specific FAF phenotypes have also been reported in chronic Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease, where fundus autofluorescence complements spectral-domain OCT in characterizing retinal pigment epithelial alterations ref [22], and in pseudoxanthoma elasticum, where FAF reveals characteristic abnormalities relevant to automated pattern recognition ref [17]. These applications indicate that FAF datasets are especially suitable for segmentation, registration, and temporal change analysis.

Field of view is another practical consideration for CAD-oriented data collection. Ultra-widefield green-light autofluorescence can capture peripheral abnormalities that may be missed on conventional posterior-pole imaging, expanding the observable disease footprint for algorithm development ref [39]. Relatedly, Optomap-based retinal screening demonstrates the feasibility of rapid widefield acquisition in acute clinical workflows, supporting deployment-oriented image triage and referral systems ref [52]. For CAD, however, FAF images are sensitive to illumination nonuniformity, media opacity, and device-dependent contrast; thus robust normalization and cross-platform harmonization are essential when integrating standard FAF, near-infrared FAF, and ultra-widefield FAF in multi-center datasets ref [21], ref [25], ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Ocular Imaging Modalities and Data Acquisition for Computer-Aided Diagnosis
subsections.subsection_title: Ocular Imaging Modalities and Data Acquisition for Computer-Aided Diagnosis - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Beyond conventional color fundus photography and structural OCT, advanced multimodal and spectrally resolved imaging expands the information available for computer-aided diagnosis. Multispectral and hyperspectral retinal imaging sample reflectance across multiple wavelengths, enabling noninvasive assessment of tissue composition, vessel contrast, and retinal oxygenation; these properties are particularly relevant for algorithms targeting metabolic or vascular abnormalities rather than morphology alone ref [32], ref [23]. Such data are inherently high-dimensional, creating opportunities for feature fusion but also imposing stricter requirements on calibration, illumination control, and dimensionality reduction during acquisition and preprocessing.

Multimodal combinations further improve lesion characterization by aligning complementary signals from different devices. Joint use of scanning laser ophthalmoscopy and spectral-domain OCT has been shown to aid phenotyping in developmental macular disorders such as foveal hypoplasia, while simultaneous eye-tracked spectral-domain OCT with real-time angiographic imaging supports early detection of neovascular activity by linking flow-related and structural cues ref [11], ref [16]. Image registration and fusion between autofluorescence and infrared channels likewise demonstrate how cross-modality alignment can enhance localization of pathological changes and provide more reliable inputs for automated analysis pipelines ref [32].

Other specialized modalities contribute additional physical contrasts that are valuable but less standardized in current CAD datasets. Adaptive-optics polarization analysis using Stokes vectors can capture microstructural and birefringence-related retinal information, and polarization-sensitive OCT has clarified the origin of atypical scanning laser polarimetry patterns, highlighting the diagnostic importance of tissue polarization behavior ref [19], ref [27]. Peripheral fundus autofluorescence has also revealed disease-associated changes in age-related macular degeneration extending beyond the macula ref [20]. For CAD systems, these modalities promise richer biomarkers, but their adoption depends on robust multimodal registration, harmonized acquisition protocols, and sufficiently annotated datasets spanning diverse devices and disease stages.

subsections.section_title: Image Processing and Structural Quantification in Ocular CAD Systems
subsections.subsection_title: Image Processing and Structural Quantification in Ocular CAD Systems - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A foundational stage in ocular CAD is the conversion of raw fundus or OCT data into delineated anatomical structures and lesion candidates. Early retinal image analysis frameworks emphasized that vessel trees, the optic disc, the optic cup, and small pathologies such as microaneurysms form the principal substrates for downstream diagnosis and risk stratification, making segmentation and structural localization central rather than auxiliary tasks ref [36], ref [22]. In fundus photography, vessel extraction has been approached through line-response operators coupled with supervised classification, enabling discrimination of thin, low-contrast vasculature from heterogeneous background tissue ref [35]. Such representations are especially important because many diagnostic biomarkers are defined not by image intensity alone, but by the geometry, caliber, and topology of extracted structures ref [36].

Beyond binary segmentation, quantitative structural measurement is critical for disease-specific CAD. Two-dimensional vessel modeling has been used to estimate retinal vessel width more robustly than simple edge picking, supporting biomarker derivation for vascular and systemic disease analysis ref [18]. For glaucoma-oriented analysis, dedicated methods for optic disc and cup segmentation from monocular color fundus images provide the basis for cup-to-disc ratio estimation and related morphological indices ref [39]. Likewise, automated detection of anatomic landmarks in retinal imagery helps normalize spatial context and constrain subsequent lesion analysis pipelines ref [22]. These steps illustrate the broader shift from pixel-level enhancement toward clinically interpretable structural quantification ref [36].

Lesion-focused processing extends this paradigm by targeting subtle abnormalities that may be poorly captured by global segmentation alone. For diabetic retinopathy screening, local rotating cross-section profile analysis has been applied to microaneurysm detection, showing how handcrafted local shape descriptors can isolate small circular lesions from vessel fragments and background texture ref [27]. In macular OCT, three-dimensional retinal layer texture analysis has been used to identify fluid-filled regions, highlighting the importance of volumetric context for quantifying intraretinal abnormalities ref [25]. Because outputs of these algorithms often serve as surrogate clinical endpoints, rigorous validation remains essential; methodological guidance has therefore stressed standardized performance assessment, reference standards, and reproducible evaluation protocols for retinal image analysis systems ref [46].

subsections.section_title: Image Processing and Structural Quantification in Ocular CAD Systems
subsections.subsection_title: Image Processing and Structural Quantification in Ocular CAD Systems - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central stage in ocular CAD is the segmentation of anatomically meaningful structures and lesions from fundus and OCT data, because subsequent diagnosis often depends on explicit geometric measurements rather than raw image appearance. In OCT, layer boundary detection and retinal thickness estimation are particularly important. Early quantitative frameworks measured retinal layer thickness directly from OCT cross-sections, establishing thickness as a reproducible structural biomarker for disease assessment ref [11]. More advanced approaches incorporated texture and shape priors to achieve robust intraretinal layer segmentation in the foveal region, improving delineation where reflectivity varies substantially across layers ref [13].

Lesion-oriented OCT processing further extended structural quantification beyond normal anatomy. Delineation of fluid-filled regions is representative of this trend, as algorithms were designed to identify and trace cystic or hyporeflective boundaries that are clinically relevant in macular edema and related disorders ref [14]. Such methods illustrate how CAD systems convert volumetric OCT intensity patterns into lesion maps, layer profiles, and summary measures that can be tracked longitudinally.

In color fundus imagery, structural quantification has focused heavily on the optic disc/nerve head and retinal vasculature. Circular Hough-transform strategies were used to localize the optic disk or optic nerve head, providing a compact but effective mechanism for initializing glaucoma-oriented analysis pipelines ref [12], ref [52]. For vascular analysis, model-based and orientation-aware tracking methods extracted vessel centerlines and trajectories under branching and curvature changes ref [18], while multiresolution Hermite representations supported finer characterization of vessel geometry across scales ref [41]. Together, these studies show that segmentation, tracking, and morphometric measurement form the backbone of image-derived biomarkers in ocular CAD systems.

subsections.section_title: Image Processing and Structural Quantification in Ocular CAD Systems
subsections.subsection_title: Image Processing and Structural Quantification in Ocular CAD Systems - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central stage of ocular CAD is the conversion of segmented anatomy into quantitative structural descriptors that can serve as biomarkers. In fundus analysis, this includes localization of the optic nerve head, explicit modeling of vessel topology, and lesion-level candidate extraction. Optic disc localization has been addressed through texture- and orientation-sensitive schemes such as Gabor filtering combined with phase portrait analysis, which are better aligned with the complex appearance variability of the disc than simple geometric assumptions alone ref [10]. At the vascular level, automatic identification of bifurcations and crossovers provides graph primitives for subsequent registration, arteriovenous analysis, and disease-oriented morphometry ref [17].

Beyond geometric segmentation, several works emphasize higher-order vascular quantification. Fractal analysis has been proposed as a robust summary of retinal vascular complexity, with methodological attention to skeletonization, scale dependence, and reproducibility of the estimated fractal dimension ref [16]. Relatedly, integrity analysis of the parafoveal capillary network also uses fractal dimension to characterize microvascular rarefaction and organization loss, illustrating how image processing outputs can be transformed into clinically interpretable biomarkers rather than remaining purely visual results ref [43]. For diabetic retinopathy screening, local lesion quantification is equally important; rotating cross-section models for microaneurysm detection exemplify how shape-constrained analysis can isolate subtle red lesions from confounding vascular fragments and background texture ref [47].

In glaucoma and macular disease, structural quantification increasingly relies on volumetric imaging. A digital stereo image analyzer was developed to derive automated three-dimensional measures of optic disc deformation, supporting objective assessment of glaucomatous structural change ref [28]. For OCT, broad reviews of retinal segmentation algorithms show that reliable boundary extraction is the prerequisite for thickness, layer continuity, and deformation measurements ref [9]. This principle is operationalized in automated macular layer segmentation frameworks, where quantitative evaluation of layer delineation accuracy directly conditions the validity of downstream biomarkers used in CAD pipelines ref [30]. Together, these studies show that structural quantification is not a single algorithmic step, but a cascade from image enhancement and segmentation to topological, fractal, lesion-based, and 3-D morphometric readouts.

subsections.section_title: Image Processing and Structural Quantification in Ocular CAD Systems
subsections.subsection_title: Image Processing and Structural Quantification in Ocular CAD Systems - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Structural quantification in ocular CAD often depends on reliable localization of salient landmarks and vascular networks before disease-specific measurements are computed. Fast anatomical localization methods for the optic disc and fovea provide a geometric scaffold for downstream analysis, reducing search space and improving consistency in screening pipelines ref [35]. In parallel, vessel extraction remains a foundational preprocessing step; edge-enhancement with object classification and multiscale enhancement coupled with second-order local entropy illustrate two efficient strategies for recovering vessel trees across varying calibers and contrast conditions in fundus images ref [48], ref [51].

Once these structures are delineated, CAD systems derive quantitative biomarkers that summarize clinically meaningful morphology. For glaucoma-oriented analysis, automated cup-to-disc ratio estimation frameworks such as ARGALI translate optic nerve head segmentation into a direct structural indicator of disc excavation ref [45]. For microvascular assessment, automated segmentation of retinal capillary perfusion maps enables fractal analysis, providing compact descriptors of branching complexity and perfusion integrity that are useful for characterizing vascular remodeling ref [41]. Sequence-based analysis further extends quantification beyond single images by jointly modeling vascular and nonvascular changes over time, supporting longitudinal assessment of retinal pathology progression ref [21].

Collectively, these studies show that structural quantification is not a single operation but a cascade: landmark detection, vessel or disc/cup segmentation, and extraction of interpretable geometric or topological descriptors. Such pipelines convert raw retinal imagery into compact biomarkers, including cup-to-disc ratio, vessel map morphology, and fractal measures, that can be integrated into higher-level CAD systems for screening, staging, and follow-up ref [21], ref [35], ref [41], ref [45], ref [48], ref [51].

subsections.section_title: Image Processing and Structural Quantification in Ocular CAD Systems
subsections.subsection_title: Image Processing and Structural Quantification in Ocular CAD Systems - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A complementary branch of ocular CAD focuses on structural quantification of the retinal vasculature after segmentation, converting vessel maps into interpretable biomarkers such as caliber, branching topology, tortuosity, and geometric complexity. Early frameworks for automatic vascular tree identification emphasized extraction of connected vessel structures and graph-like organization, enabling downstream measurement of branching patterns and network architecture rather than pixel-level detection alone ref [28]. Similar pipelines linked vessel tree segmentation with assessment of neural-layer deterioration, highlighting how vascular representations can serve as indirect markers of tissue damage in retinal disease analysis ref [9].

Among derived descriptors, tortuosity and vessel-shape metrics have been particularly important because they capture subtle remodeling not reflected by width alone. Automated tortuosity analysis on color fundus images demonstrated the feasibility of reproducible vessel-by-vessel quantification in large image sets, supporting CAD systems for vascular abnormality screening and follow-up ref [49]. Related shape-analysis approaches further showed that glaucomatous change can be characterized through alterations in retinal vessel geometry, suggesting that vascular deformation may provide adjunctive evidence beyond optic disc-based measures ref [57].

Global network descriptors have also been explored to summarize vascular complexity. Fractal analysis revealed reduced retinal vascular complexity in CADASIL, illustrating the value of scale-invariant descriptors for detecting systemic or neurovascular pathology in ocular images ref [59]. More generally, robust fractal-based retinal analysis has been proposed as a standardized way to quantify vessel pattern organization and improve reproducibility across imaging studies ref [48]. Longitudinal CAD systems extend these ideas by measuring temporal changes in retinal structure and lesion configuration in serial images, as demonstrated for maculopathy monitoring, where quantitative comparison across visits supports objective disease progression assessment ref [43].

subsections.section_title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Frameworks for Ocular Disease Classification
subsections.subsection_title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Frameworks for Ocular Disease Classification - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Early computer-aided diagnosis frameworks for ocular disease classification were largely built on a classical pipeline: image preprocessing, anatomical structure detection, handcrafted lesion description, and statistical decision making. Broad reviews of retinal image analysis emphasized this modular design, in which clinically meaningful structures such as vessels, optic disc, cup, and candidate lesions were first isolated before classification was attempted ref [38]. This paradigm also aligns with general medical image classification surveys, where feature engineering and explicit pattern modeling preceded end-to-end learning and offered greater transparency in low-data settings ref [48].

Within this framework, disease-oriented systems typically relied on task-specific detectors. For diabetic retinopathy, statistical classification was coupled with image-derived lesion cues for screening, while microaneurysm analysis used local rotating cross-section profiles to encode small vascular abnormalities with greater specificity ref [23], ref [27]. For glaucoma assessment, optic disc and cup segmentation provided structural biomarkers that could be transformed into discriminative measurements such as cup-to-disc ratio ref [64]. More generally, automatic detection of anatomic retinal structures supplied the spatial priors needed to constrain downstream classifiers and reduce false positives from normal background variation ref [22].

A notable strength of these traditional AI frameworks is that they made validation and data quality explicit components of the diagnostic pipeline. Image quality assessment methods, including no-reference schemes based on vessel segmentation, addressed the fact that poor fundus quality can degrade both feature extraction and classification reliability ref [42]. Likewise, methodological work on validation highlighted the need for standardized reference annotations, fair performance comparison, and careful separation of training and test data in retinal algorithm studies ref [46]. Although later data-driven methods reduced dependence on handcrafted descriptors, these early machine learning systems established the core principles of feature interpretability, clinically grounded modeling, and rigorous evaluation that still underpin ocular disease classification.

subsections.section_title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Frameworks for Ocular Disease Classification
subsections.subsection_title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Frameworks for Ocular Disease Classification - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A prominent intermediate paradigm between purely handcrafted screening systems and end-to-end deep learning is the feature-engineering pipeline, in which anatomically meaningful structures are first localized or segmented and then converted into discriminative descriptors for classification. In fundus analysis, this strategy has relied on explicit detection of the optic disc or optic nerve head using shape-driven transforms such as circular Hough voting, which stabilizes downstream glaucoma-related measurements and lesion context modeling ref [12], ref [52]. Likewise, vessel extraction and tracking methods based on multi-orientation analysis provide structured representations of the retinal vascular tree, enabling later computation of caliber, branching, and tortuosity features for disease inference ref [18].

The same design philosophy is evident in vessel-type and layer-aware models. Artery-vein classification systems transform segmented vasculature into semantic vascular graphs, enriching feature spaces with hemodynamically relevant information beyond simple vessel presence ref [14]. In OCT, statistical texture-and-shape models for intraretinal layer segmentation support the derivation of thickness, boundary regularity, and topographic descriptors that are more directly related to pathology than raw intensities alone ref [13]. Similar segmentation-first formulations have been used to delineate fluid-filled retinal regions, where boundary-aware representations capture disease burden in macular disorders and can be supplied to subsequent machine learning classifiers ref [67].

For glaucoma, such engineered representations have been translated into explicit diagnostic rules or conventional classifiers. Segmented macular SD-OCT scans have been used for glaucoma discrimination through measurements derived from retinal substructures rather than unconstrained image appearance ref [21], while three-dimensional minimum-distance mapping from OCT volumes offers another handcrafted geometric descriptor for diagnosis ref [40]. Collectively, these studies illustrate a clinically interpretable framework: domain knowledge guides localization and segmentation, engineered biomarkers are computed from anatomically constrained regions, and classification is performed on compact, explainable feature sets. Although less data-hungry than modern deep networks, these pipelines remain sensitive to error propagation from early preprocessing stages.

subsections.section_title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Frameworks for Ocular Disease Classification
subsections.subsection_title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Frameworks for Ocular Disease Classification - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A useful intermediate paradigm between purely handcrafted pipelines and end-to-end deep learning is feature-driven classification built on anatomically meaningful representations. In retinal imaging, this strategy typically decomposes diagnosis into lesion or structure extraction followed by statistical learning. For example, optic nerve head localization using Gabor filters and phase-portrait analysis provides a geometric prior for downstream glaucoma-oriented assessment, while vessel-tree bifurcation and crossover characterization encodes topological information that can support disease-sensitive vascular analysis ref [10], ref [17]. Likewise, fractal descriptors of the retinal vasculature offer compact summaries of branching complexity that have been associated with pathological change and can serve as inputs to conventional classifiers ref [16].

In OCT-based CAD, classical machine learning has often relied on explicit texture and layer features rather than raw-volume learning. SVM-based texture classification demonstrated that retinal tissue patterns in OCT can be discriminated with carefully engineered descriptors, illustrating the continued relevance of supervised kernel methods when datasets are limited or labels are expensive ref [32]. Segmentation is especially important in this context: reviews of OCT retinal segmentation and quantitative evaluations of macular layer delineation show that thickness, boundary, and layer-integrity measurements can be transformed into disease biomarkers for subsequent classification or staging ref [9], ref [30].

This framework is also evident in diabetic retinopathy screening, where microaneurysm detectors based on rotating cross-section models act as lesion-specific feature extractors, and referral-oriented systems aggregate such outputs into clinically actionable decisions ref [47], ref [48]. Across these studies, the dominant methodological pattern is modular: preprocess, detect structures or lesions, derive interpretable features, and classify. Although such pipelines may underperform modern deep networks on very large datasets, they remain valuable because they are computationally efficient, easier to validate component-wise, and more transparent in linking image evidence to diagnostic decisions ref [10], ref [32], ref [48].

subsections.section_title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Frameworks for Ocular Disease Classification
subsections.subsection_title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Frameworks for Ocular Disease Classification - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A practically important strand of ocular diagnosis frameworks is the feature-engineering pipeline, in which anatomical structures and lesion candidates are first localized or segmented and then converted into quantitative descriptors for classification. This paradigm is attractive in ophthalmology because many disease criteria are inherently morphometric, such as optic disc–fovea geometry, cup-to-disc ratio, vascular caliber, and lesion distribution. Fast localization of key landmarks has therefore been used as an enabling stage for screening systems, reducing search space and improving robustness of downstream decision modules ref [35].

Disease-specific implementations illustrate how these handcrafted representations support interpretable prediction. In age-related macular degeneration, severity grading from fundus photographs has been automated through image-derived phenotypic measurements linked to clinically meaningful staging rules ref [28]. For diabetic retinopathy, automatic analysis pipelines combine lesion-sensitive preprocessing with detection of pathological signs in fundus images to derive case-level decisions ref [36]. In glaucoma, cup-to-disc ratio estimation remains a canonical example of a clinically transparent biomarker, and systems such as ARGALI explicitly translate optic nerve head measurements into diagnostic support outputs ref [45].

Vascular analysis is another core component of classical machine learning workflows, since vessel topology and appearance influence both quality assessment and disease discrimination. Edge-enhancement and object-classification strategies have been proposed for vessel extraction ref [48], while multi-scale enhancement combined with second-order local entropy enables faster and more discriminative vessel segmentation ref [51]. These modules are rarely final classifiers by themselves; rather, they provide structured inputs for subsequent learning algorithms, illustrating a broader design principle in ocular CAD: interpretable intermediate representations often compensate for limited data, but their performance depends strongly on the accuracy of upstream localization and segmentation stages ref [35], ref [45].

subsections.section_title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Frameworks for Ocular Disease Classification
subsections.subsection_title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Frameworks for Ocular Disease Classification - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A complementary line of work within ocular CAD emphasizes mid-level representations, deployment settings, and longitudinal analysis rather than end-to-end classification alone. Early systems integrated automated retinal image analysis into networked or web-based workflows, anticipating scalable screening services and remote decision support ref [18]. Such system-level studies are important because model utility in ophthalmology depends not only on discrimination accuracy, but also on interoperability, turnaround time, and the ability to support repeated assessments over time.

Before contemporary deep learning, many frameworks relied on engineered descriptors tailored to lesion appearance and vascular morphology. Bright-lesion analysis was addressed through histogram-based exudate detection and through visual-saliency strategies that attempted to separate clinically relevant lesions from confounders such as drusen or illumination artifacts ref [40], ref [13]. More generic image-representation paradigms also emerged; notably, bag-of-words encoding provided a statistical texture framework for distinguishing retinal images containing exudates from those with drusen, illustrating an early shift from rigid rule-based pipelines toward learned visual vocabularies ref [39]. In parallel, multiscale AM-FM analysis offered a signal-processing foundation for capturing textural and structural variations across retinal pathology, while texton-based vessel segmentation demonstrated how learned texture primitives could improve anatomical parsing as an upstream step for diagnosis ref [44], ref [51].

These frameworks also highlight the value of interpretable biomarkers and temporal validation. Quantitative tracking of maculopathy across visits linked CAD to disease progression analysis rather than single-image labeling ref [43]. Likewise, vascular tortuosity estimation provided explicit geometric markers that can support glaucoma, retinopathy, and systemic disease studies while remaining clinically interpretable ref [49]. Taken together, these studies represent an important methodological bridge: they combine handcrafted features, statistical learning, and deployable analysis pipelines, and they foreshadow current interest in explainable, workflow-aware, and longitudinally robust AI for ocular disease classification ref [18], ref [43], ref [49].

subsections.section_title: Vascular and Geometric Biomarkers for Ocular and Systemic Disease Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Vascular and Geometric Biomarkers for Ocular and Systemic Disease Assessment - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Retinal vascular geometry provides a noninvasive window onto microvascular health, making fundus analysis particularly valuable for computer-aided phenotyping of both ocular and systemic disease. Foundational reviews emphasize that vessel caliber, branching structure, tortuosity, and global network complexity can be extracted from routine retinal images and translated into quantitative biomarkers with potential diagnostic and prognostic value ref [78], ref [82], ref [28]. Within CAD pipelines, accurate vessel segmentation and centerline localization are therefore not merely preprocessing steps, but prerequisites for reproducible biomarker estimation.

Among these markers, vessel caliber remains the most clinically established. Automated or semi-automated measurement strategies, including 2-D vessel profile modeling, have improved the precision of width estimation from fundus photographs ref [18]. Clinically, altered arteriolar and venular diameters have been associated with major cardiovascular outcomes: meta-analytic evidence links retinal vessel caliber to coronary heart disease risk ref [9], while population-based data from the Multiethnic Study of Atherosclerosis associate narrower arterioles and wider venules with incident hypertension risk ref [49]. These findings have motivated substantial interest in standardizing retinal vascular caliber assessment for broader risk stratification ref [28].

Beyond diameter, higher-order geometric descriptors capture complementary aspects of vascular remodeling. Multifractal analysis has been proposed to characterize the hierarchical complexity of retinal vessel networks, offering a richer representation than single-scale summary measures ref [31]. Such vascular biomarkers are also being investigated in neurodegeneration, where retinal microvascular alterations may support early detection and monitoring of Alzheimer’s disease ref [15]. Collectively, this literature positions retinal vascular analysis as a bridge between ophthalmic CAD and systemic disease modeling, with future progress depending on robust image acquisition, harmonized measurement protocols, and longitudinal validation ref [82], ref [28].

subsections.section_title: Vascular and Geometric Biomarkers for Ocular and Systemic Disease Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Vascular and Geometric Biomarkers for Ocular and Systemic Disease Assessment - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Beyond static caliber measurements, computer-aided diagnosis increasingly exploits vessel topology, artery–vein identity, and local geometry as higher-order biomarkers. Reliable extraction of these descriptors depends on robust vascular parsing, including vessel tracking across complex orientations, explicit modeling of centerlines and widths, and artery/vein discrimination for branch-specific analysis of remodeling patterns in disease ref [18], ref [41], ref [14]. These algorithmic steps are essential because geometric biomarkers such as branching configuration, tortuosity, and tree complexity are highly sensitive to segmentation and labeling errors.

Among structural biomarkers, fractal and multiscale descriptors have been particularly informative for systemic disease assessment. Retinal vascular fractal alterations have been associated with microvascular and macrovascular complications in type 1 diabetes, supporting the view that reduced vascular complexity captures cumulative systemic injury rather than merely local retinal change ref [19]. Such findings motivate CAD pipelines that quantify network sparsity, branching loss, and hierarchy disruption from fundus or angiographic images as compact indicators of vascular health.

Functional vascular imaging further broadens biomarker scope by measuring perfusion and flow rather than morphology alone. Temporal analysis of laser speckle patterns has enabled retinal blood-flow estimation, while phase-resolved OCT and optical microangiography provide depth-resolved visualization of retinal and choroidal circulation with increasingly wide fields of view ref [23], ref [37], ref [50]. In glaucoma, the clinical value of these metrics is reinforced by reported relationships among visual field loss, blood-flow parameters, and neural structural measurements, suggesting that combined geometric and hemodynamic biomarkers may improve disease staging and progression monitoring ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Vascular and Geometric Biomarkers for Ocular and Systemic Disease Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Vascular and Geometric Biomarkers for Ocular and Systemic Disease Assessment - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Beyond vessel caliber alone, higher-order geometric descriptors such as fractal dimension, bifurcation topology, and capillary network integrity have emerged as informative biomarkers of microvascular health. Fractal analysis provides a compact summary of branching complexity, but its diagnostic utility depends strongly on segmentation quality and analysis protocol; accordingly, robust methodological formulations were developed to improve reproducibility in retinal vascular fractal measurement ref [16]. Related work on parafoveal capillary imaging further showed that fractal dimension can quantify local capillary integrity, supporting its use as a sensitive marker of microvascular rarefaction or disorganization in macular-centered disease assessment ref [43].

Structural characterization of vascular junctions offers a complementary geometric perspective. Automated detection and characterization of bifurcations and crossovers enable extraction of branch angles, junction density, and tree topology, which are relevant to remodeling processes in hypertension, diabetes, and other vasculopathies ref [17]. At finer scales, adaptive optics studies of patients with type 1 diabetes and nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy demonstrated that capillary-level abnormalities can be measured directly, indicating that subtle microvascular remodeling precedes or accompanies clinically visible retinopathy ref [38]. Together, these studies highlight how computer-aided analysis is moving from coarse vessel segmentation toward quantitative phenotyping of the full vascular architecture.

Importantly, such retinal biomarkers are not restricted to ophthalmic endpoints. Associations between retinal vascular caliber and systemic biomarkers of oxidative stress and inflammation suggest that ocular vascular measurements can act as accessible surrogates of broader cardiovascular risk and endothelial dysfunction ref [51]. In this context, combining caliber, fractal complexity, and junctional geometry may yield more robust multidimensional signatures than any single metric alone, improving CAD systems for both ocular disease stratification and systemic disease screening ref [16], ref [17], ref [43], ref [51].

subsections.section_title: Vascular and Geometric Biomarkers for Ocular and Systemic Disease Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Vascular and Geometric Biomarkers for Ocular and Systemic Disease Assessment - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Beyond static caliber and tortuosity descriptors, functional vascular biomarkers derived from advanced ocular imaging provide complementary evidence about perfusion, oxygen delivery, and vessel wall properties. Hyperspectral analysis has been used to estimate oxygen saturation in optic nerve head structures, enabling spatially resolved assessment of local metabolic status that may reflect ischemic or glaucomatous stress rather than morphology alone ref [34]. Polarimetric imaging likewise adds sensitivity to blood-column and vessel-related optical signatures, supporting vessel quantification under contrast conditions that differ from conventional color fundus photography ref [37]. These developments align with broader retinovascular physiology studies emphasizing that hemodynamic dysregulation and oxygenation abnormalities are central biomarkers of ocular and systemic microvascular disease ref [40].

Such functional markers are particularly valuable when integrated with structural vascular readouts. Comparative work between colour Doppler imaging and scanning laser fluorescein angiography illustrates how flow-related measurements can reveal abnormalities in glaucoma that are not fully captured by anatomical inspection alone ref [47]. At the image-analysis level, longitudinal fundus sequence methods that jointly model vascular and nonvascular change offer a route to tracking disease progression by combining vessel alterations with surrounding retinal context ref [21]. In parallel, high-resolution non-invasive capillary perfusion maps have enabled automated segmentation and fractal analysis of capillary beds, extending biomarker extraction from large vessels to microvascular networks with finer physiological relevance ref [41].

These richer biomarkers still depend on reliable vessel delineation. Classical extraction pipelines based on edge enhancement and object classification established practical vessel maps from fundus photographs ref [48], while later multiscale enhancement and second-order local entropy methods improved efficiency and robustness across varying vessel widths and contrast levels ref [51]. In survey terms, the key trend is a shift from purely geometric descriptors toward multimodal, function-aware biomarkers in which segmentation, perfusion mapping, oxygenation estimation, and longitudinal integration jointly strengthen computer-aided assessment of both ocular pathology and systemic vascular dysfunction ref [21], ref [34], ref [41].

subsections.section_title: Vascular and Geometric Biomarkers for Ocular and Systemic Disease Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Vascular and Geometric Biomarkers for Ocular and Systemic Disease Assessment - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Beyond caliber measurements, computer-aided retinal analysis increasingly exploits higher-order geometric and functional biomarkers, including tortuosity, branching topology, fractal complexity, vessel-shape descriptors, and oxygenation-related signals. Automated extraction of vascular tree structure enables quantitative characterization of connectivity and local geometry at scale, providing the computational basis for reproducible biomarker discovery in fundus images ref [28]. Tortuosity analysis is a representative example: automated methods have shown that vessel curvature and path irregularity can be robustly measured from color retinal photographs and used as disease-relevant descriptors rather than merely qualitative observations ref [49].

These biomarkers have shown relevance across both ocular and systemic disorders. In glaucoma, vessel-shape analysis has been proposed as a marker of glaucomatous change, complementing conventional structural indicators of optic nerve damage ref [57]. Hemodynamic alterations are likewise important, as studies combining retrobulbar blood-flow assessment with morphometric optic disc analysis in primary open-angle glaucoma suggest that vascular compromise and structural deformation should be interpreted jointly ref [17]. At the systemic level, retinal vessel analysis has detected microvascular changes in hypercholesterolemic patients and their modification after LDL apheresis, illustrating the sensitivity of retinal biomarkers to systemic metabolic state and treatment effects ref [59].

Network-complexity metrics further broaden this translational role. Reduced fractal complexity has been reported in CADASIL, supporting the retina as a surrogate window onto cerebral small-vessel disease ref [60]. More generally, retinal microvascular signs have been discussed as potential indicators of distinct stroke mechanisms, reinforcing their value for neurovascular stratification ref [36]. Functional biomarkers are also emerging: hyperspectral approaches for retinal oxygen saturation analysis have been examined for validity, indicating that geometric and metabolic vascular measurements may ultimately be integrated in CAD systems for multidimensional risk assessment ref [23].

subsections.section_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis Across Major Ocular Disease Categories
subsections.subsection_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis Across Major Ocular Disease Categories - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Glaucoma has been one of the most intensively studied targets for computer-aided diagnosis because its structural damage can be quantified from both fundus photography and optical coherence tomography (OCT). In this category, CAD systems typically focus on biomarkers linked to retinal ganglion cell degeneration, including optic disc cupping, retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thinning, and macular ganglion cell complex loss. Early image-analysis pipelines emphasized automated optic disc and cup delineation from color fundus images to derive cup-to-disc ratio and related morphometric indicators, establishing a practical route for screening in settings where OCT is unavailable ref [101].

With the adoption of Fourier-domain and spectral-domain OCT, glaucoma CAD increasingly shifted toward layer-resolved quantitative assessment. Studies reported that macular ganglion cell loss is detectable with Fourier-domain OCT and can complement traditional peripapillary analysis ref [99]. The diagnostic value of ganglion cell complex measurements is strengthened by documented structure-function relationships, indicating that OCT-derived structural parameters can serve as computational surrogates for visual field damage ref [19]. Subsequent macular imaging work further showed that spectral-domain OCT provides useful diagnostic accuracy for glaucoma discrimination, supporting CAD models that integrate macular thickness maps and regional asymmetry features ref [44].

A critical consideration in glaucoma CAD is distinguishing disease-related change from normal aging. Normative analyses have demonstrated age-related RNFL decay in healthy eyes ref [11], with prospective spectral-domain OCT studies confirming measurable age-associated loss over time ref [20]. Longitudinal CAD therefore benefits from progression-oriented modeling rather than single-visit thresholds alone. Pattern analysis of RNFL progression and map-based evaluation of RNFL thickness distributions have been shown to improve glaucoma detection and monitoring, motivating algorithms that exploit spatially localized change, temporal trends, and deviation from age-adjusted norms ref [32], ref [40].

subsections.section_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis Across Major Ocular Disease Categories
subsections.subsection_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis Across Major Ocular Disease Categories - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Glaucoma has been one of the most extensively studied targets for computer-aided diagnosis because its structural damage can be quantified from the optic nerve head (ONH), peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL), and macular ganglion-cell regions. Clinical imaging reports have emphasized that ONH and RNFL analysis are central to objective glaucoma assessment, while CAD systems operationalize these biomarkers through automated segmentation, thickness profiling, and deviation analysis from normative patterns ref [15], ref [32]. Early CAD strategies therefore focused on extracting cup-disc morphology from fundus images and RNFL measurements from OCT to support screening and case discrimination.

With the maturation of spectral-domain and 3-D OCT, glaucoma CAD has shifted toward finer structural phenotyping. RNFL imaging by SD-OCT improved the sensitivity of structural assessment, and 3-D approaches such as minimum-distance mapping further exploited volumetric geometry for diagnosis ref [39], ref [40]. Beyond peripapillary scans, macular analysis also proved informative: segmented Cirrus SD-OCT macular scans enabled discrimination of glaucomatous eyes by quantifying inner retinal damage that may complement RNFL-based criteria ref [21]. These developments illustrate a broader algorithmic trend from handcrafted global indices toward layer-specific, regionally resolved, and volumetric descriptors.

An important direction in glaucoma CAD is multimodal structure-function integration. Mapping visual field loss to peripapillary RNFL sectors provides a principled way to link functional impairment with localized structural damage ref [106]. Likewise, studies relating visual field, ocular blood flow, and neural structure underscore that robust diagnostic models may benefit from combining imaging biomarkers with hemodynamic and psychophysical measurements rather than relying on a single modality ref [25]. Overall, glaucoma CAD aims not only to classify disease presence, but also to detect early change, localize damage, and support longitudinal monitoring of progression.

subsections.section_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis Across Major Ocular Disease Categories
subsections.subsection_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis Across Major Ocular Disease Categories - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
For macular and outer-retinal disorders, computer-aided diagnosis has centered on multimodal characterization of structural disruption rather than solely global screening. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is the dominant substrate because it resolves photoreceptor, retinal pigment epithelium, and chorioretinal interface abnormalities in three dimensions, enabling quantitative assessment of layer integrity, drusen-related deformation, cystic change, and atrophic thinning ref [14], ref [35]. Reviews of OCT segmentation methods show that automated delineation of intraretinal and outer-retinal boundaries is a prerequisite for disease-specific biomarkers such as layer thickness, reflectivity profiles, and volumetric lesion burden ref [9], while comparative evaluations of macular layer segmentation demonstrate how performance at the boundary level directly affects downstream CAD reliability ref [30].

Beyond generic segmentation, disease-oriented CAD for macular degeneration and inherited macular dystrophies increasingly exploits modality-specific signatures. Fundus autofluorescence supports quantification of geographic atrophy extent and progression in advanced age-related macular degeneration, making lesion border extraction and intensity-based analysis clinically valuable for monitoring rather than simple case detection ref [26]. Multimodal fundus imaging has similarly been used in Best vitelliform macular dystrophy to relate complementary en face and tomographic findings, illustrating a broader CAD trend toward fusing phenotypic cues across autofluorescence, color imaging, and OCT ref [37]. Texture-based learning on OCT, including SVM-based classification, further indicates that local appearance descriptors can distinguish pathological retinal microstructure when explicit lesion models are difficult to specify ref [32].

Another important direction is microvascular analysis of the parafoveal region, where capillary dropout and architectural rarefaction may accompany macular disease. Integrity assessment using fractal-dimension measures provides a compact descriptor of parafoveal network complexity and offers a bridge between structural imaging and perfusion-sensitive CAD pipelines ref [43]. Taken together, CAD in this disease category is moving from single-image lesion detection toward integrated quantification of layer morphology, atrophic area, and parafoveal vascular organization, with 3-D OCT serving as the principal computational backbone ref [14], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis Across Major Ocular Disease Categories
subsections.subsection_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis Across Major Ocular Disease Categories - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Inherited and less common retinal disorders form an important but methodologically distinct CAD category because diagnosis often depends on subtle phenotype characterization rather than high-volume screening. In this setting, fundus autofluorescence (FAF), near-infrared autofluorescence, and multimodal structure–function correlation are especially valuable. For Stargardt disease, computational analysis of autofluorescent images has been used to delineate atrophic lesions and quantify growth over time, illustrating how CAD can support longitudinal monitoring and trial endpoints rather than only binary classification ref [21]. Related work on near-infrared autofluorescent signal localization further clarifies disease-relevant contrast mechanisms that can be exploited for automated feature extraction in macular dystrophies and retinal pigment epithelium disorders ref [25].

Phenotype-driven CAD is also relevant in rarer dystrophies and macular disorders where multimodal biomarkers are heterogeneous. Detailed structure–function analysis in autosomal recessive bestrophinopathy highlights the need to integrate retinal morphology with functional impairment, suggesting a role for systems that jointly analyze imaging and clinical measurements ref [12]. In type 2 idiopathic macular telangiectasia, retinal crystals provide a small but specific imaging sign whose automated detection could improve sensitivity for early or atypical presentations ref [14]. Likewise, fundus autofluorescence abnormalities in pseudoxanthoma elasticum and genotype-defined macular dystrophy phenotypes such as MCDR3 underscore the value of CAD tools designed for pattern recognition across inherited retinal disease spectra rather than disease-specific single biomarkers ref [17], ref [27].

A related extension of this subgroup is ocular oncology, where the diagnostic target shifts from retinal lesions to intraocular tumors. Diffusion-weighted imaging of ocular melanoma shows that non-retinal modalities can contribute quantitative contrast for lesion characterization, broadening CAD beyond fundus and OCT pipelines toward multimodal decision support across ocular disease categories ref [38]. Overall, for rare retinal dystrophies and ocular tumors, the main CAD objective is not mass screening but robust lesion localization, phenotype stratification, and reproducible progression assessment across diverse imaging modalities ref [21], ref [12], ref [17], ref [25], ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis Across Major Ocular Disease Categories
subsections.subsection_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis Across Major Ocular Disease Categories - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Macular disorders constitute a heterogeneous CAD target that spans age-related macular degeneration (AMD), epiretinal membrane, neovascular maculopathy, and inherited macular dystrophies. In this category, the dominant computational objective is not only lesion detection but also quantitative characterization of morphologic change on OCT and multimodal retinal imaging. Early work emphasized longitudinal computer-aided assessment of maculopathy progression, establishing registration and change-analysis pipelines for serial retinal images and thereby supporting follow-up-oriented CAD rather than single-visit classification alone [43].

For AMD, CAD systems have largely centered on OCT-derived structural biomarkers such as pigment epithelial detachment, retinal thickness alterations, and subretinal or intraretinal neovascular activity. Three-dimensional OCT analysis of pigment epithelial detachment illustrates the importance of volumetric representation and topographic quantification for characterizing disease burden [38]. Multimodal imaging of early type 3 neovascularization further shows how eye-tracked SD-OCT combined with angiographic information can localize subtle vascular complexes that may be difficult to appreciate on any single modality [16]. Peripheral autofluorescence abnormalities in AMD also suggest that CAD pipelines should extend beyond the macula and exploit ultra-widefield phenotyping when building screening or staging models [20].

In parallel, CAD for other macular diseases increasingly integrates structural and functional endpoints. OCT-based prediction of visual outcomes in macular disease highlights the clinical shift from descriptive image analysis toward prognosis-oriented modeling [5]. En face retinal surface OCT in epiretinal membrane surgery demonstrates how surface-oriented representations can better capture tractional distortion patterns relevant to surgical planning [7]. For inherited disease, functional analysis of retinal flecks in Stargardt disease underscores the need for CAD systems that jointly quantify lesion appearance and visual consequence rather than relying on morphology alone [46]. Overall, macular CAD is moving toward multimodal, longitudinal, and outcome-aware frameworks tailored to diverse disease mechanisms [5, 7, 16, 20, 38, 43, 46].

subsections.section_title: Translational Challenges, Clinical Utility, and Future Directions in Ocular CAD
subsections.subsection_title: Translational Challenges, Clinical Utility, and Future Directions in Ocular CAD - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A primary translational barrier in ocular CAD is the lack of acquisition and annotation standardization across imaging devices and clinical sites. Digital fundus imaging varies substantially with respect to field of view, illumination, color balance, compression, and operator technique, all of which affect downstream algorithm robustness and comparability in screening workflows ref [33], ref [118]. Similar concerns are even more pronounced in OCT, where segmentation outputs and quantitative biomarkers depend on scanner hardware, scan protocols, and software definitions of retinal boundaries ref [119], ref [21], ref [38]. As a result, models trained on narrowly curated datasets often show diminished reliability when transferred to routine practice.

Image quality control and validation methodology therefore become central to clinical utility rather than auxiliary preprocessing steps. No-reference fundus quality assessment has been proposed as a practical mechanism to identify ungradable images before automated interpretation, reducing preventable errors caused by poor contrast or vessel visibility ref [42]. At the same time, the validation literature emphasizes that algorithm assessment must move beyond single-center accuracy reports toward transparent protocols, representative case mixes, and explicit definitions of reference standard and failure modes ref [46]. These requirements are consistent with broader lessons from medical image AI, where apparent performance can be inflated by dataset bias, limited external testing, and task formulations that do not reflect real clinical decision pathways ref [48].

Taken together, these studies suggest that the first step toward deployable ocular CAD is not simply designing stronger classifiers, but building reproducible evaluation ecosystems. Standardized imaging pipelines, cross-device calibration for structural measurements, routine image-quality triage, and prospectively designed validation benchmarks are prerequisites for trustworthy deployment in glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, and macular disease applications ref [21], ref [38], ref [42], ref [46].

subsections.section_title: Translational Challenges, Clinical Utility, and Future Directions in Ocular CAD
subsections.subsection_title: Translational Challenges, Clinical Utility, and Future Directions in Ocular CAD - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central translational challenge for ocular CAD is the lack of measurement standardization across imaging devices, acquisition settings, and patient populations. This issue is especially evident in OCT-based structural assessment, where retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) and optic nerve head parameters are influenced not only by disease status but also by age, scan quality, segmentation behavior, and instrument-specific variability. Clinical reports and guideline-oriented reviews have therefore emphasized that CAD outputs must be interpreted within validated imaging protocols rather than treated as device-agnostic biomarkers ref [15], ref [28], ref [32].

In glaucoma, the clinical utility of CAD depends on whether automated analysis can robustly distinguish true neuroretinal change from normal anatomical variation. Studies of optic disc and RNFL imaging show that structural markers are diagnostically valuable, but their performance is tightly linked to reproducibility and normative referencing, particularly when spectral-domain OCT is used for early detection or longitudinal monitoring ref [32], ref [39], ref [15]. From a deployment perspective, this implies that future systems should incorporate uncertainty estimation, quality control, and site-specific calibration to reduce false alerts arising from acquisition artifacts or inter-device differences ref [28], ref [39].

At the same time, expanding CAD beyond tertiary centers requires hardware pathways compatible with screening and resource-limited settings. Portable imaging platforms, including mobile phone-based retinal cameras, illustrate how lower-cost acquisition may broaden access, but they also introduce further heterogeneity in field of view, illumination, and image quality that algorithms must accommodate ref [105]. A similar translational lesson comes from diabetic macular edema, where OCT has become central to management because it links imaging biomarkers to treatment decisions; here, the next generation of CAD should move from single-task detection toward clinically actionable triage, progression assessment, and multimodal decision support ref [43].

subsections.section_title: Translational Challenges, Clinical Utility, and Future Directions in Ocular CAD
subsections.subsection_title: Translational Challenges, Clinical Utility, and Future Directions in Ocular CAD - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A major future direction for ocular CAD is integration with teleophthalmology, where clinical value depends not only on algorithmic accuracy but also on triage relevance, image acquisition variability, and workflow compatibility. Early remote screening studies in retinopathy of prematurity and diabetic retinopathy showed that image-based assessment can achieve clinically meaningful discrimination relative to standard examination, supporting the feasibility of distributed diagnostic pathways ref [22], ref [23]. In this setting, CAD is especially useful when framed as referral support rather than autonomous diagnosis, consistent with work on automatic diabetic retinopathy systems that explicitly optimized the need-for-referral decision ref [48].

Multimodal imaging further expands translational utility because many ocular diseases are not adequately characterized by a single modality. Clinical studies of inherited and degenerative retinal disorders have demonstrated that combining complementary fundus-based channels can reveal lesion extent, phenotype heterogeneity, and disease activity more effectively than isolated imaging alone ref [37], ref [39]. For CAD, this implies that future systems should move from single-image classifiers toward fusion models that jointly analyze color, autofluorescence, infrared, and structural data, while preserving interpretability for ophthalmologists.

The same shift is evident in OCT-centered diagnosis. Three-dimensional OCT provides richer structural context than individual B-scans, but its benefit in practice depends on reliable volumetric segmentation, standardization across devices, and robust handling of pathology-induced artifacts ref [14], ref [9]. Thus, clinically deployable ocular CAD will likely be multimodal, triage-aware, and embedded in telemedicine infrastructures, with performance judged by referral safety, workflow efficiency, and generalizability rather than benchmark accuracy alone ref [22], ref [23], ref [48].

subsections.section_title: Translational Challenges, Clinical Utility, and Future Directions in Ocular CAD
subsections.subsection_title: Translational Challenges, Clinical Utility, and Future Directions in Ocular CAD - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A central translational issue for ocular CAD is hardware and acquisition heterogeneity. Differences among fundus camera systems alter field of view, color rendition, resolution, and artifact profiles, which can shift algorithm performance when models are exported beyond the development site ref [70]. Similar concerns arise in ultra-widefield screening, where systems such as Optomap expand peripheral visualization and casualty screening utility, but also introduce image characteristics that are not interchangeable with conventional fundus photographs ref [52]. Consequently, clinically useful CAD will require device-aware validation, explicit reporting of imaging conditions, and calibration strategies that reduce domain shift across acquisition platforms.

The same need for standardization is evident in OCT-based CAD. Spectral-domain OCT has become integral to glaucoma diagnosis and management, yet its outputs are influenced by segmentation conventions, scan protocols, and instrument-specific thickness measurements ref [22]. In neovascular age-related macular degeneration, retinal thickness parameters were specifically evaluated for clinical-trial use, underscoring that quantitative biomarkers must be reproducible and clinically interpretable before they can support automated decision-making ref [24]. These observations imply that translational CAD should be benchmarked not only on diagnostic accuracy, but also on repeatability, longitudinal consistency, and compatibility with established endpoints used in practice and trials.

Future clinical utility will also depend on workflow integration and scalable deployment. Web-based analysis environments such as Sirius illustrate how remote retinal image processing can support distributed screening and second-opinion models, but they also foreground requirements for interoperability, secure data exchange, and quality control ref [52]. Disease-specific systems for diabetic retinopathy and AMD severity grading demonstrate that robust performance depends on reliable preprocessing, including optic disc and fovea localization, as well as lesion-sensitive classification pipelines ref [36], ref [28], ref [35]. Overall, the next generation of ocular CAD is likely to be multimodal, platform-aware, and service-oriented, moving from isolated algorithms toward clinically embedded systems that connect imaging devices, quantitative biomarkers, and teleophthalmology infrastructures.

subsections.section_title: Translational Challenges, Clinical Utility, and Future Directions in Ocular CAD
subsections.subsection_title: Translational Challenges, Clinical Utility, and Future Directions in Ocular CAD - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A major future direction for ocular CAD is the transition from single-image classification toward integrated, multimodal, and prognostic decision support. Clinical ophthalmology already relies on complementary signals from OCT, fundus photography, autofluorescence, infrared imaging, angiographic views, and emerging spectral modalities; accordingly, CAD systems must fuse structural, functional, and molecularly sensitive information rather than optimize on isolated benchmarks. Early demonstrations of multimodal retinal assessment, including combined scanning laser ophthalmoscope and spectral-domain OCT imaging, highlight how cross-modality interpretation can improve phenotypic characterization in conditions such as foveal hypoplasia and neovascular disease ref [11], ref [16]. Image registration and fusion studies further show that clinically meaningful correspondence across autofluorescent and infrared channels is technically achievable, which is essential for longitudinal monitoring and multimodal biomarker extraction ref [32].

Beyond diagnosis, translational utility will increasingly depend on whether CAD can predict treatment response and visual prognosis. OCT-based work on visual outcome prediction in macular disease illustrates this shift from detection to management-oriented modeling ref [72]. However, deployment-quality prognostic systems require robust control of acquisition variability and artifacts. Studies of OCT frame averaging demonstrate that preprocessing choices materially affect image appearance and downstream analysis, while optic nerve head analyses have documented artifacts that can confound glaucoma-related interpretation in both diseased and normal eyes ref [35], ref [50]. These findings underscore that future systems must explicitly model uncertainty, image quality, and device-specific failure modes before they can be trusted in routine care.

Scalable implementation also points toward networked and remote CAD ecosystems. Early internet-based retinal image analysis platforms anticipated contemporary cloud and teleophthalmology workflows, suggesting a pathway for extending specialist-grade analytics to screening and underserved settings ref [18]. At the same time, multispectral retinal imaging offers a non-invasive route to richer tissue characterization than standard color imaging alone, potentially expanding CAD from morphology-centered recognition toward physiology-aware assessment ref [34]. Taken together, the field is moving toward multimodal, interoperable, and prognostic ocular CAD, but success will depend on standardized acquisition, reliable cross-device fusion, and clinically validated workflows that demonstrate benefit beyond algorithmic accuracy alone ref [72], ref [18], ref [32].
